Teaching the Harness: Student-Aware Skill Transfer for LLM Agents

Chang Liu Affiliation: Colorado School of Mines Affiliation: Golden, CO, USA Email: liuchang@mines.edu    Bo Wu Affiliation: Colorado School of Mines Affiliation: Golden, CO, USA Email: bwu@mines.edu
Abstract

Effective teaching requires reasoning about the learner as well as the task, a capacity that Theory of Mind describes as inferring another agent’s latent state from its behavior. We ask whether a stronger LLM teaches a fixed student better when it applies this principle. The student is an LLM agent acting through a harness that fixes its tools, context, and action budget, so a procedure that helps one model can exhaust the budget of another. We introduce Student-Aware Teaching (SAT). The teacher builds a learner model that pairs an empirical profile with hypotheses about the student’s limitations, tests these hypotheses with diagnostic probes, and writes reusable skills for the diagnosed failures. A skill enters the library only after it raises success on matched development tasks. With Claude-Sonnet-5 teaching DeepSeek-V4-Flash, SAT reaches 86.46% task success across four primary runs, leading both a profile-free teacher with the same framework (81.04%) and the untaught student (75.00%) in each run. Removing the analytical learner model lowers both prediction and success, and under misleading learner profiles none of the 48 candidate skills passes admission. When DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Gemini-3.8-Flash exchange libraries, each performs better with its own. Saved libraries keep average gains of up to 11.1 points after the teacher leaves. The benefit depends on a student that can follow instructions and a deployment route that delivers them.

   

Keywords LLM agents ⋅\cdot Agent skills ⋅\cdot Machine teaching ⋅\cdot Theory of mind ⋅\cdot Agent harnesses

1 Introduction

Many large language model (LLM) agents now pair a model with a harness (Yao et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025a; Anthropic, ; OpenAI, ). A harness is the software layer around the model. It supplies tools, runs a multi-step action loop, manages the context, and caps how many actions the model may take. These components make execution far more complicated than answering a single prompt. A model may know how to restock an inventory and still fail because it spends its allowed actions querying items one at a time. A model may know how to rename files and still leave a nested directory untouched. Many agent failures are failures of execution through a specific harness. This shift also complicates how competence is transferred. Knowledge distillation and machine teaching mostly target the model itself, by updating its weights or choosing its training examples (Hinton et al., 2015; Hsieh et al., 2023; Zhu, 2015). Yet smaller models are increasingly deployed inside harnesses while stronger models remain available at higher cost (Belcak et al., 2025), and many deployed models cannot be retrained by their users. The model is also not the only component that can learn. The harness can receive knowledge from an external source as reusable procedures, often called skills, which it loads at run time to guide a fixed model’s actions. Skills are readable, cheap to store, and easy to replace. Recent work already learns such skills from execution (Zheng et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026; Alzubi et al., 2026; Ni et al., 2026). These methods mostly learn from the agent’s own failures or optimize skills against a task metric, and less attention has gone to what a teacher should know about the particular model and harness it teaches. We study this question with skills that the harness supplies as advisory context, keeping the model weights and harness code fixed.

The hard part is deciding what a skill should say. Advice to verify every intermediate result helps a student that loses track of its state. The same advice exhausts the action budget of a student that already verifies too often. A useful lesson therefore depends on the learner. Theory of Mind describes the capacity to infer the latent state of another agent from its behavior and to use that inference to anticipate what it will do (Premack and Woodruff, 1978). Developmental research links this capacity to teaching, since a teacher must reason about what the learner knows and where it will go wrong (Strauss et al., 2002; Wellman and Lagattuta, 2004). In practice this reasoning forms a teaching loop. The teacher keeps a working estimate of the student’s state, updates it from the student’s responses, and uses it to choose the next lesson, so the quality of teaching depends on the quality of that estimate. This view fits harness teaching especially well. The limits that matter live in the execution procedure, such as how many updates fit in the action budget, and a teacher can see them only by modeling how this student acts through this harness. We therefore ask: does a teacher model write better skills when it first models the student it teaches?

Student-Aware Teaching (SAT) takes this teaching loop as its design basis. The learner is a student model paired with its harness. The teacher maintains a learner model with two parts: an empirical profile records what the student does, and an analytical learner model holds hypotheses about why it fails. The teacher tests these hypotheses with controlled probes, such as inventories of increasing size, and writes skills for the diagnosed failures. A candidate enters the library only if it raises the student’s success on matched development tasks. After teaching, the teacher leaves and the student works with the saved library alone. Our study focuses on three research questions.

  • •

    RQ1 (teaching quality). Does an explicit model of the learner produce better skills than teaching from the same types of execution feedback alone?

  • •

    RQ2 (teaching content). What does a student-aware teacher teach differently, and are its lessons specific to their student?

  • •

    RQ3 (realizing the benefit). Does the curriculum keep helping after the teacher leaves, and which delivery routes, students, and harnesses turn it into a gain?

We compare SAT with an agnostic teacher that uses the same skill generation and admission framework and learns from its own failed trajectories, but has no learner model or probes. SAT leads it in all four primary runs (RQ1). False-profile and library-swap controls provide additional evidence that teaching benefits from learner-specific information (RQ1, RQ2). Saved libraries keep average gains of 5.6 to 11.1 points with the teacher absent. The gain is realized when the delivery route suits the student and the student can execute procedures. Mid-sized open students benefit most, while the smallest cannot (RQ3). Our contributions are as follows.

  • •

    We formulate agent teaching as building a validated skill library for a fixed model and harness, separating teaching quality from how skills are delivered after the teacher leaves.

  • •

    We propose SAT, which puts a Theory-of-Mind view of teaching into practice. Its learner model pairs an empirical profile with analytical hypotheses, probes test those hypotheses, and matched admission tests validate each lesson.

  • •

    We show that learner-conditioned teaching improves a fixed student over profile-free teaching, particularly when failures arise from execution constraints. Controls with misleading profiles and exchanged libraries support the role of learner-specific information, and student capability and skill delivery determine whether the gain is realized.

2 Related Work

Learner modeling in teaching.

Theory of Mind research argues that a teacher must reason about a learner’s knowledge, ignorance, and misconceptions (Strauss et al., 2002; Wellman and Lagattuta, 2004). Knowledge tracing and machine teaching formalize instruction for a modeled learner (Corbett and Anderson, 1994; Zhu, 2015), and Iterative Machine Teaching and its black-box extension choose examples from the learner’s estimated state (Liu et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2018). Machine Theory of Mind and false-belief tests for LLMs study whether models can predict other agents (Rabinowitz et al., 2018; Kosinski, 2024). SAT uses the idea in a functional sense. Its learner is an LLM paired with its harness, so the state to estimate includes execution limits such as how many updates fit in the budget.

Transferring competence to a fixed model.

Knowledge distillation and its variants train a student on teacher predictions, rationales, or feedback on the student’s own samples (Hinton et al., 2015; Hsieh et al., 2023; Agarwal et al., 2024). These methods update weights, while SAT writes an external library that can be inspected and edited and that reaches students with inaccessible weights. Prompt optimization refines instructions or pipelines from textual critiques, task metrics, or execution traces (Pryzant et al., 2023; Yuksekgonul et al., 2024; Khattab et al., 2023; Agrawal et al., 2026). Our agnostic baseline generates skills from traces, verifier outcomes, and development feedback. SAT adds an explicit learner model that guides diagnostic probes and skill generation.

Agent memory, skills, and harnesses.

Experience-based methods store lessons from an agent’s own runs as verbal feedback, insights, workflows, or playbooks (Shinn et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Ouyang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026). Skill libraries range from executable code (Wang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025b) to skills that stronger agents pass to weaker ones (Zheng et al., 2025). SkillOpt and EvoSkill revise natural-language skills for a frozen agent from execution failures and keep an edit only when held-out validation improves (Yang et al., 2026; Alzubi et al., 2026). Trace2Skill consolidates lessons from many trajectories into declarative skills that transfer across models (Ni et al., 2026). Other work shows that the agent-computer interface shapes performance (Yao et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2024) and searches agent, workflow, or harness code (Hu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2026), including harnesses built by strong models for weaker targets (Qian et al., 2026). SAT asks what an explicit student model and diagnostic probes add to learning skills from failures. Our library exchange tests how much of a learned library is specific to its student. Table 1 summarizes how SAT relates to each family.

3 Student-Aware Teaching

SAT treats teaching as an iterative loop between a stronger teacher and a fixed learner (Figure 1). In each round the student attempts teaching tasks, and the teacher updates its model of the student, tests it with diagnostic probes, and writes candidate skills that must pass an admission test. After preparation the teacher leaves, and a selector delivers the saved skills to new tasks.

3.1 Problem: teaching a fixed learner

Let S=(Ms,H)S=(M_{s},H) denote a learner formed by a student model MsM_{s} and its execution harness HH. For task xx and supplied skills LxL_{x}, the learner produces a trajectory τ∼S⁡(x,Lx)\tau\sim S(x,L_{x}), and a verifier returns V⁡(x,τ)∈{0,1}V(x,\tau)\in\{0,1\}. A teaching policy π\pi maps preparation evidence EE to a skill library ℒ=π⁡(E)\mathcal{L}=\pi(E). After preparation, the teacher leaves and a selector gg chooses which skills accompany each task. Expected performance is

J⁡(S,ℒ,g)=𝔼x∼𝒟τ∼S⁡(x,g⁡(x,ℒ))​[V⁡(x,τ)].J(S,\mathcal{L},g)=\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim\mathcal{D}\\ \tau\sim S(x,g(x,\mathcal{L}))\end{subarray}}[V(x,\tau)]. (1)

Teaching aims to raise JJ under a finite preparation budget, with later instances drawn from task families seen during preparation.

We compare two policies that differ in what the teacher knows about the learner. Both receive the same types of evidence from their own runs: task descriptions, verifier outcomes, execution traces, and development feedback. We write this evidence as EagnE_{\mathrm{agn}} for the agnostic condition and EE for the aware condition. The aware policy maintains a learner model σ\sigma and can request diagnostic probes, so it receives Eaware=E∪{σ,probes}E_{\mathrm{aware}}=E\cup\{\sigma,\text{probes}\} and can predict how this particular student will fail before writing a lesson. Both policies start from the same six generic skills. Our teaching question (RQ1) asks whether J⁡(S,πaware​(Eaware),g)J(S,\pi_{\mathrm{aware}}(E_{\mathrm{aware}}),g) exceeds J⁡(S,πagn​(Eagn),g)J(S,\pi_{\mathrm{agn}}(E_{\mathrm{agn}}),g) for a fixed learner and selector. Our reuse question (RQ3) fixes the library and varies gg with the teacher absent.

3.2 From student evidence to candidate skills

Learner model.

The aware teacher maintains a learner model σ\sigma with two parts. The empirical profile records what the student does. At each round the student attempts a batch of teaching tasks with its current library, and the teacher updates category-level success statistics, failure labels, and notes (Appendix A). The analytical learner model records why the student fails. Observed failures rarely identify their own cause, so the teacher keeps hypotheses about latent execution constraints. Each hypothesis stores a proposed mechanism, a confidence, supporting evidence, and a status. For example, the teacher may hypothesize that repeated stock queries consume the action budget before all updates finish. The learner model also yields a prediction p^σ​(x)\hat{p}_{\sigma}(x) of whether the bare student will solve task xx. We score these predictions with Brier and AUROC on a fixed calibration panel.

Controlled probes as hypothesis tests.

Passive observation can support several explanations for one failure. An inventory failure may come from misreading the task, missing a deficient item, or running out of actions. SAT therefore makes learner modeling active. The teacher requests probes that vary one supported property within a task family, such as inventory size or file count. The bare student attempts each variant, which is rebuilt with its own verifier. If success falls as size grows, the evidence points to an execution-budget limit and the transition records a sampled boundary. The outcome updates the learner model and steers the teacher toward simpler procedures.

Skill generation.

The teacher proposes up to three candidate skills per round, each a short natural-language procedure with a target category and applicability metadata (Appendix A). The aware prompt receives the learner model, weak-category priorities, and probe evidence, while the agnostic prompt receives tasks and failed traces from its own condition. Both forbid copying task-specific answers. Skills are delivered as advice, and the student chooses its own actions.

3.3 Admission and deployment

A candidate ss is tested on one to four development tasks PsP_{s} from its category. Each task runs once with the candidate alone and once with an empty library. The estimated standalone utility is

U^​(s)=1|Ps|​∑x∈Ps[Y⁡(x,{s})−Y⁡(x,∅)],\widehat{U}(s)=\frac{1}{|P_{s}|}\sum_{x\in P_{s}}\left[Y(x,\{s\})-Y(x,\varnothing)\right], (2)

where YY denotes verifier acceptance. A candidate with positive utility enters the library and may replace a generic skill in its category. The library keeps a small number of active skills per category.

After preparation the teacher is removed. We study three selectors gg. Student selection asks the student to choose up to two skills from a metadata menu. Category routing matches the task’s category tag and picks up to two skills by validation utility. Flat injection supplies every active skill. No selector sees test outcomes.

4 Experimental Setup

Base harness.

Our base harness is a compact planning harness. It first asks the student for a plan and then runs a tool-calling loop of at most ten iterations. It truncates long tool observations and keeps a limited window of recent messages, so action budget and context loss are real constraints. Skills enter as advisory text ahead of the task instruction. Unless a result states another selector, skills reach the student through category routing, both during teaching and in the reported evaluations.

Tasks.

We use five task suites. A generator builds each task together with its working environment and a programmatic verifier. The suites target different ways an agent can fail inside a tight harness.

  • •

    Terminal. Shell tasks such as recursive renaming, sorted numeric merges, and staged file pipelines, which test coverage of the environment.

  • •

    Inventory API. Restocking every item below a threshold through list, query, and restock tools, which tests action economy.

  • •

    Arithmetic. Word problems on discounts, mixtures, and rates, which test task semantics.

  • •

    Python code. Function implementation and bug repair, which test program correctness.

  • •

    Dependent workflows. Chains of file stages that each consume the previous output, which test state tracking.

Main setting and experiments.

Runs S1 through S4 use Claude-Sonnet-5 (Anthropic, 2026) as teacher and DeepSeek-V4-Flash (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026) as student. Each run uses 60 teaching tasks, 30 development tasks, and four teaching rounds. The final evaluation executes 60 held-out tasks, twelve per suite, twice each. Every experiment compares no skill, agnostic teaching, and aware teaching (SAT) under the same student and harness. RQ1 adds two component ablations and a false-profile control, which replaces the learner model with a frozen and deliberately wrong profile. RQ2 analyzes skill bodies, an eight-round extended run, and a library swap between DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Gemini-3.8-Flash (Doshi and Popa, 2026). RQ3 evaluates frozen libraries under three selectors with the teacher absent and varies the student across Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025a), Qwen2.5-Instruct (Yang et al., 2025b), GPT-5.4-Mini (OpenAI, 2026), and Gemini-3.8-Flash. Further experiments cover production harnesses, MATH and GSM8K subsets (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Cobbe et al., 2021), and self-teaching. Only S1 through S4 enter the primary mean. We report acceptance, the percentage of held-out executions whose final result passes the task’s verifier (Appendix J).

5 Results

We present results in the order of the three research questions. Unless noted otherwise, all numbers are final-round acceptance in the base harness with category routing.

5.1 RQ1: Studying the student makes a better teacher

Aware teaching wins every primary run. Table 2 reports the primary comparison. SAT reaches 86.46% mean acceptance, compared with 81.04% for agnostic teaching and 75.00% without skills. Its advantage over agnostic teaching is positive in all four runs and averages 5.42 points, and its gain over no skill averages 11.46 points. Across these four runs, SAT also has lower observed dispersion, with a standard deviation of 1.25 points against 5.58.

The gain concentrates where execution is hard. The largest aware advantages appear in terminal tasks (71.88% against 62.50%) and inventory tasks (86.46% against 76.04%), which require the student to cover an environment or complete many updates within a fixed action budget. Arithmetic, where the student mainly needs a formula, slightly favors agnostic teaching. Learner modeling thus helps most when failures come from how the student acts through the harness.

Component ablations are consistent with benefits from modeling and probing. Table 3 varies what the teacher knows about its student. Final aware acceptance is 83.3% in both ablated configurations, compared with 87.5% for full SAT. Removing the analytical learner model also raises the teacher’s Brier score for predicting student success from 0.041 to 0.180. Removing probes leaves prediction accurate, which suggests that prediction accuracy alone does not capture all information relevant to teaching. Probes supply measured limits, such as the inventory size at which the student breaks. Because each configuration ran as its own job with its own baselines, these differences are indicative. Both ablated teachers still exceed their own no-skill and agnostic baselines.

Misleading learner profiles derail teaching. To test sensitivity to inaccurate learner information, we supply deliberately overestimating and underestimating profiles and keep everything else fixed. One profile describes DeepSeek-V4-Flash as a frontier model for which step limits hardly matter. The other describes it as a tiny model that needs exhaustive scaffolding. Both stay frozen while the teacher observes the real student’s trajectories. Under both profiles, none of the 48 generated candidates passes the admission test, so the libraries retain only the six initial generic skills. The teacher’s predictions also degrade. The underestimating teacher ends with Brier near 0.75 and AUROC below 0.3, so its predictions run against the student’s real outcomes. Final acceptance averages 75.0% and 79.2%, within the range of the untaught student in the primary runs. The false-profile teachers spend $0.36 to $0.41 per run, similar to the $0.39 of the correct-profile teacher.

5.2 RQ2: The aware teacher writes lessons that fit the learner

From a diagnosed budget limit to a bulk procedure. The clearest sequence comes from a Qwen3-8B student taught by Qwen3-14B. After two inventory failures at the action limit, the aware teacher probes inventory size and finds that the student passes with two items and fails at five or more. It then writes a procedure that begins with one full stock query, which passes three of four admission tasks where the bare student passes none. The agnostic plan checks stock item by item (Table 4). Final inventory acceptance is 91.67% with aware teaching, 0% with agnostic teaching, and 8.33% without skills. The same repair appears in S4, where a bulk snapshot skill lifts inventory acceptance to 79.17% against 50.00% agnostic. In these cases the learner model changes the procedure itself: per-item or bulk queries, shallow or recursive discovery, and early or deferred checks (Appendix C).

From a missed nested file to recursive coverage. The extended run shows the teacher adapting over eight rounds (Figure 2). In round six, a teaching attempt leaves a nested file unrenamed. The aware teacher responds with a skill that enumerates matching files recursively and checks that no original extension remains. Renaming acceptance rises from 30% to 100% and stays there for the final three rounds, while the agnostic student keeps a shallow glob and passes two of ten executions. Overall, aware acceptance climbs from 78.3% to 84.3%, against 80.7% agnostic and 78.0% without skills. The aware teacher also predicts its student better. Its Brier score is lower in every round, and its predictions separate passing from failing panel tasks perfectly (AUROC 1.0) in six of eight rounds. Its admitted skills have mean standalone utility 0.58 against 0.35 for agnostic skills.

Probe results enter the lesson. The extended run also shows a measured limit passing directly into skill text. In round three, an inventory probe finds that the bare student succeeds with eight items and fails with twelve and sixteen. The skill written in round four cites the twelve-item failure explicitly. It advises one consolidated stock query, progress tracking across updates, and a final check only when the budget allows. The lesson thus builds on an observed failure from the diagnostic probe. A later probe in the same run passes at all tested sizes, so such boundaries depend on the sampled instances.

Awareness changes what the curriculum emphasizes. We annotated the complete main-setting skill bodies with five overlapping functional labels (Appendix C). Half of the aware skills teach environment coverage, compared with one in ten agnostic skills. Both curricula give similar amounts of advice on execution economy and verification, yet they differ in when and what to check. Some aware skills defer checks to save actions, while the Qwen3-8B skills add explicit checks during or after stock updates. Verification timing is thus a teaching decision that depends on the learner.

Libraries carry student-specific advantages. If aware lessons encode properties of one learner, they should fit that learner better than another. We exchange the aware libraries of DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Gemini-3.8-Flash, both taught by the same teacher in the same harness (Table 5). Both students perform better with their own libraries than with the exchanged libraries across the evaluated routes. Category routing fixes retrieval and isolates library content. Under this route DeepSeek-V4-Flash reaches 93.3% with its own library and 83.3% with Gemini’s, a difference of 10.0 points with paired interval [2.5,18.3][2.5,18.3]. Several exchanged libraries still help their recipients, and Gemini-3.8-Flash shows smaller margins near its ceiling. The pattern suggests that learner-conditioned teaching produces libraries with some student-specific advantages (Appendix H).

5.3 RQ3: Realizing the benefit after the teacher leaves

Teaching pays off only if the saved curriculum reaches a student that can use it. We examine three conditions in turn: the absence of the teacher, the route that delivers skills, and the student and harness that receive them.

The curriculum outlives the teacher. Table 6 freezes saved aware libraries and removes the teacher. Every DeepSeek-V4-Flash library improves the student under category routing and flat injection. Across L1 to L3, mean gains are 5.6 points with student selection, 8.6 with category routing, and 11.1 with flat injection. The library from the extended run keeps gains of 5.7 to 7.7 points. Teaching is thus a one-time investment that keeps paying off without further teacher calls.

Delivery can erase a good curriculum. The local students reveal two failure modes. Qwen3-8B never selects a skill in any of its 120 student-selection executions and gains nothing. Category routing and flat injection deliver the same library and recover a 15-point gain. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct shows the opposite pattern. It gains 8.3 points when it chooses its own skills and loses 14.2 points when it receives the whole library. The best route therefore depends on the student, and a deployment should choose it with the student in mind.

Mid-sized students gain the most. Table 7 varies the student and teacher. With a Qwen3-14B teacher, Qwen3-8B rises from 38.3% without skills to 53.3% with aware teaching, while agnostic teaching falls to 33.3%. A Qwen3-32B teacher also gives this student a clear aware gain. The smallest students do not respond. Qwen3-1.7B stays at 11.7% in every condition and retains no learned skill, and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct changes little across two runs. Strong API students sit at the other end. GPT-5.4-Mini and Gemini-3.8-Flash start near 88% and gain at most five points from either teacher, and agnostic teaching matches or slightly exceeds aware teaching for both. For GPT-5.4-Mini, the aware teacher predicts its student better in two of three runs while accuracy ties (Appendix F). Procedural teaching thus needs a student that can execute procedures and still has room to improve.

Portability and exploratory settings. SAT can also be applied through the native interfaces of four production harnesses: Codex (OpenAI, ), Pi (Earendil Works, ), OpenCode (OpenCode, ), and Claude Code (Anthropic, ). Skills are supplied as task context, while each harness retains its own tools and execution workflow. The harnesses differ from the base harness and from each other, so we compare each condition only with the same harness without skills. Final point estimates favor aware teaching over no skill in every harness, by 1.0 to 5.2 points (Appendix I). Appendix E further reports exploratory results on small public mathematics subsets and a self-teaching comparison. On MATH and GSM8K subsets, aware teaching exceeds agnostic teaching by 8.3 points on each and matches or exceeds both baselines in all five runs. In the self-teaching comparison, the student’s own backbone is already a useful teacher, since self-improvement adds 9.7 points over no skill. Replacing the student’s self-generated skills with those from Claude-Sonnet-5, while keeping the same inputs, adds a further 1.4 points, which is one additional accepted execution among 72 test executions.

6 Discussion

What the learner model adds. Both teachers see the student fail, and both can write useful procedures. The learner model changes which procedure the teacher chooses. A failed inventory task is consistent with misreading the task, missing an item, or running out of actions, and each reading suggests a different lesson. When the teacher’s model and probes point to the action budget, it writes a bulk query. When they point to incomplete coverage, it writes recursive discovery. The results line up with this account. Gains concentrate in suites where execution constraints bind, ablating the analytical model or the probes lowers acceptance, misleading profiles yield no admissible skill, and each student does better with its own library. In the language of Theory of Mind, the teacher benefits from anticipating how this particular student will act. None of these controls alone isolates learner modeling as the only source of the gain, but they point in the same direction as the main comparison.

Scope. Most evidence comes from one teacher and student pair in one base harness, with few seeds for the controls and deliberately extreme false profiles. Deployment results depend on the selector, and the production and exploratory experiments carry the caveats stated beside them. The learner model also has natural limits: it cannot help a student too small to execute procedures, and it adds little for a student near ceiling. Matched replays of teaching evidence, milder profile errors, more seeds, and dedicated studies in production harnesses are the natural next steps.

7 Conclusion

We asked whether a teacher model teaches better when it first models its student. Across four primary runs, Student-Aware Teaching improves over profile-free teaching, with the largest gains on tasks that involve constrained execution. Its saved libraries keep helping after the teacher leaves. Ablations, misleading profiles, and exchanged libraries all support the role of learner-specific information, which Theory of Mind research places at the center of human teaching. Modeling whom it is teaching can help a teacher decide which procedures to teach.

AI Use Statement

We used generative AI as part of the research pipeline described in the paper, including model-based generation and annotation procedures. We also used generative AI tools to polish the manuscript and check its clarity and consistency. All research design, analyses, interpretations, and conclusions were reviewed and verified by the authors, who take full responsibility for the final content.

Reproducibility Statement

Section 3 specifies the teaching and deployment protocol, and Appendix A provides implementation details such as prompt limits and admission rules. Appendix B describes the base harness, task generators, and split sizes. Appendices D and E report per-route and per-run results with paired intervals. Appendix C gives the annotation codebook and paired skill artifacts. Appendix G reports the full extended trajectory and the paired bootstrap procedure. Appendices H and I describe the learner-specificity controls and the production-harness protocol. Appendix J lists the cost ledgers and category-level results.

Appendix A Additional Method Details

A.1 Learner model

For each teaching round, the student attempts a batch using its current library. The aware profile tracks successes and failures per category. For category cc, its Beta-Bernoulli summary begins with αc=βc=1\alpha_{c}=\beta_{c}=1. Observed successes increase αc\alpha_{c} and failures increase βc\beta_{c}. The profile also stores failure counts and short teacher notes. Because the library changes across rounds, these statistics describe the student under an evolving curriculum. They should be read as estimates of the taught student, which differs from the bare model.

The analytical learner model stores a textual mechanism summary and a bounded set of hypotheses. Each hypothesis includes a claim, a confidence, supporting evidence, and a status. Additional fields hold inferred or measured task boundaries. The teacher uses this state to target a recurring execution problem. For example, it may suspect that repeated stock queries exhaust the action budget before all updates are issued. Analytical updates are stored separately from the empirical profile, which lets us examine observed behavior and its proposed explanation separately.

How the learner model changes a teaching decision.

The empirical profile includes category performance, observed failure modes, teacher notes, and probe outcomes. These components can guide teaching before a detailed explanation is available. A low inventory success rate can motivate a lesson on completing stock updates within the action budget. Repeated intermediate reads can motivate consolidated execution. Missing nested files can motivate recursive discovery. The same task can support several plausible lessons. A student that omits necessary checks may need an explicit completion test, while a student that repeatedly checks finished work may need fewer checks. The learner model tells the teacher which of these lessons fits.

A.2 Controlled probes

Probes vary a supported task property while preserving the task family. Implemented axes include inventory size and file count for search tasks. The generator rebuilds each variant and recomputes its verifier. The bare student attempts a small ordered set of property values. Analytical hypotheses can guide these diagnostics, and empirical failures can trigger probes before any explanation exists. A transition from observed success to observed failure is recorded as a sampled boundary. For example, passing at 12 items and failing at 16 brackets a transition over those tested instances. All-pass, all-fail, and nonmonotonic sweeps are recorded as inconclusive.

A.3 Skill generation and representation

The teacher proposes up to three skills per round. The prompt requests concise reusable procedures and prohibits copying task-specific answers. Each body is limited to 900 characters. Skills have four native types: content, process, affordance, and plan. A record stores its body and target category together with harness scope, provenance, and a validation summary. Applicability metadata can name task families and failure modes, and an optional field holds a student-specific rationale.

The aware teacher receives the statistical profile, the available analytical learner model, and a focus list of weak categories. The agnostic teacher receives tasks, verifier information, eligible execution traces, and prior skills from its own condition. A generation request includes up to six task descriptions and four failed traces. Plan records can contain structured directives. In all complete packages reported here the delivery mode is advice, so the harness injects skill text and the student chooses its actions. The implementation also supports controller-enforced plans, which we leave for future evaluation.

A.4 Empirical skill admission

A candidate skill ss is evaluated on up to four development tasks matching its category. Each task is executed with the candidate and with an empty library, giving the standalone utility in Equation 2. Candidate validation uses temperature zero. A candidate with no matched task is rejected, and a positive estimate admits the skill. Admission can deactivate a generic seed in the same category, and the library keeps at most two active skills per category. Up to two off-category tasks estimate interference with the same paired comparison. This quantity is logged for analysis only. Because the gate measures each candidate against an empty library, we evaluate complete libraries separately at test time.

A.5 Selection after teaching

The saved artifact contains the library and the learner model. The deployment experiment removes the teacher and evaluates three routes.

  • •

    Student selection. The student reads a metadata menu and returns at most two valid skill identifiers. It sees the task’s category label, the first 400 characters of the instruction, and a short preview of each body. Selected bodies are injected before execution.

  • •

    Category routing. A deterministic rule matches the task’s category or suite tag and selects up to two skills by validation utility. Logs call this route oracle.

  • •

    Flat injection. Every active skill is supplied to the student.

Category routing uses task metadata and has no access to test outcomes. Deployment on untagged tasks is a natural extension.

A.6 Evaluating the student model

The teacher can predict bare-student success on calibration tasks. Brier score measures squared probability error. Predictions are scored on a panel of ten calibration tasks. Task success remains the primary measure of whether a curriculum helps the student.

Appendix B Base Harness and Task Suites

Base harness.

The compact planning harness runs one episode per task. It first asks the student for a short plan, then enters a tool-calling loop of at most ten iterations. Each iteration lets the student call one tool or finish. Tool observations are truncated to 400 characters. The context keeps the system message and the six most recent conversational messages, so earlier observations drop out of view in long episodes. Supplied skills are injected as advisory text before the task instruction, and the student decides whether and how to follow them. The harness itself never changes during teaching. The same harness executes teaching, development, probe, and test tasks for every condition.

Task generation.

Each suite has a seeded generator that builds a task instruction, its working environment, and a programmatic verifier. A frozen collection fixes the teaching, development, and test splits before any teaching begins, and all conditions within an experiment share one collection. Probes call the same generators with one property changed, such as the number of inventory items or the number of files to search, and rebuild the verifier for each variant. Table 8 lists the suites and Table 9 gives split sizes.

Generic initial skills.

Agnostic and aware teaching start from the same six generic skills. The first three are count matching lines, do stages in order, and check then restock. The other three are filter rows carefully, merge and sort, and rename matching files. Learned skills can replace them within a category.

Appendix C Curriculum Analysis and Paired Skill Artifacts

C.1 Three views of a curriculum

The S1 through S4 libraries contain 28 active learned skills, with 13 agnostic and 15 aware. Table 10 reports their native types. Aware teaching retains more process skills, and agnostic teaching uses more affordance skills. Complete bodies are available for ten agnostic and twelve aware skills from S2 through S4. S1 contributes metadata for its remaining six learned skills. The Qwen3 package adds one agnostic and four aware skills, which we use for category counts and paired cases. Native type records the teacher’s representation choice, task category records where a skill is assigned, and functional labels record the behavior requested in the body.

Within S2 through S4, aware teaching deactivates seven of eighteen generic initial skills and agnostic teaching deactivates five. Each aware package retains two rename procedures.

C.2 Functional annotation

Table 11 defines five functional labels. Coding uses the complete active body and permits overlapping labels. Annotations come from a single model-assisted pass and are recorded per skill. Counts describe this collection and treat skills within a library as related observations.

Within the complete bodies, the main-setting aware curriculum places more skills on environment coverage. Both conditions contain substantial advice about execution economy and verification. Native type can hide this overlap, since a plan and an affordance record both teach batching for dependent stages. Aware metadata names the compact planning harness as the skill’s scope, while agnostic metadata typically declares general applicability.

C.3 Allocation across tasks

Table 13 shows the target categories of complete bodies. Six of twelve main-setting aware skills target renaming, and each aware library retains two of them. Four of ten agnostic skills target dependent workflows. All seven learned rename skills include environment coverage and verification. Both sorted-merge skills discuss semantics and verification.

C.4 Paired teaching cases

We inspect paired cases through four kinds of evidence: the recorded student difficulty, the generated procedure, its validation, and final execution outcomes. Table 14 summarizes them.

S4: a repair for a limited action budget.

In S4, a first-round inventory teaching attempt reaches the ten-step limit before completion. The aware teacher then generates a bulk stock-check procedure. It receives standalone utility 0.50 on four matched development tasks and replaces the generic inventory skill. The agnostic library keeps the generic instruction to check stock and restock deficient items. The aware body specifies one stock snapshot followed by only the necessary updates, and it explicitly links redundant per-item queries to the student’s action budget. The saved profile records difficulty with repeated verification and names consolidated stock checks as a useful procedure. Final inventory acceptance is 79.17% for aware teaching, 50.00% for agnostic teaching, and 62.50% without skills. Execution records show per-item stock queries under the agnostic library and bulk queries under the aware skill.

Qwen3: a probe precedes the lesson.

The Qwen3-8B student’s first teaching batch includes two inventory step-limit failures and a missing completion marker. Before the first candidate is generated, the aware log records an inventory probe. The student passes at two items and fails at five or more. The teacher then generates a skill beginning with a full stock query. Its standalone validation succeeds on three of four matched tasks, while the bare comparison succeeds on none. The two retained aware inventory skills start with bulk retrieval and specify update verification. Their final inventory acceptance is 91.67%, compared with 0% for agnostic teaching and 8.33% without skills. For one matched task, the agnostic record contains three SKU-list calls and seven per-item stock calls with no restock call. The aware record contains two bulk stock calls and one restock call. Both aware executions of that task pass, and both agnostic executions fail. This case gives the most complete chain in our artifacts, from observed failure through probing and validation to final success.

S3: choosing which verification to keep.

S3 shows a subtler difference. Its initial inventory attempts include a step-limit failure and an understocked item. Both teachers eventually produce a bulk-read procedure. The agnostic body skips routine verification unless an update looks wrong. The aware body performs a final full-stock check and repairs remaining shortages before writing the completion marker. Both skills have standalone utility 0.25 on four matched tasks. Final inventory acceptance is 95.83% with aware teaching and 91.67% with agnostic teaching. The aware procedure keeps one well-placed check while still reducing repeated discovery calls.

S1: batching dependent stages.

S1 retains an aware chain skill with standalone utility 0.50 that computes chain stages in one shell call. The agnostic library retains an affordance skill for simple single-purpose commands. Final dependent-workflow acceptance is 95.83% for aware teaching and 75.00% for agnostic teaching. Inventory acceptance is also higher under aware teaching, at 91.67% against 62.50%.

Useful lessons from agnostic teaching.

Agnostic teaching also finds real procedural knowledge. An agnostic merge skill in S2 through S4 notices that the supplied merge inputs lack trailing newlines. Concatenating the files can join the last integer of one file to the first integer of the next, so the skill passes both files directly to the sorting command. Arithmetic in the main comparison also slightly favors agnostic teaching. The advantage of learner modeling is largest where failures depend on how the student acts through the harness.

C.5 Verification as a conditional teaching decision

Several chain skills in S2 through S4 combine reading, computation, and writing in one shell action. They discourage a separate read for every intermediate value and defer verification. The Qwen3 aware chain skill asks the student to check each output file before proceeding, and its inventory skills add explicit checks after updates. Within one main-setting aware library, the chain skill suppresses intermediate checks while the pipeline skill asks for one check per stage. These bodies expose a concrete teaching choice about which checks a student should perform under a constrained budget. A label such as verification is therefore most informative when paired with its timing and target.

C.6 Admission support

The aware rename procedures repeatedly address recursive discovery and exact extension replacement. Eight of twelve complete main-setting aware skills were admitted using one matched task, and the other four used four tasks. For agnostic teaching, three skills used one task, one used two, and six used four. Development splits contain one rename task each, which is reused across rename candidates. Larger development pools would sharpen utility estimates for narrow categories.

Appendix D Teacher-Free Deployment Details

Table 15 gives absolute teacher-free results for the three DeepSeek libraries and the two local configurations. Each route executes its own no-skill baseline. L2 is the library from S4. None of these deployment scores enters Table 2.

Table 16 reports teacher-free evaluation of the library from the extended run. All three routes improve on the 78.0% no-skill baseline, and each interval excludes zero.

Appendix E Public Subsets and Self-Teaching

The two experiments in this section are exploratory. Their caveats are stated beside each result.

Public subsets.

The source lists contain 200 unique GSM8K questions and 500 unique MATH problems. The loader partitions each shuffled list into 50% teaching, 20% probe, and 30% test pools. Each experiment uses twelve items from each pool, and every test item is executed twice. The answer verifier accepts a submission that contains the gold answer as a substring. This lenient rule applies equally to all conditions. Table 18 reports each run.

Aware teaching matches or exceeds both baselines in all five runs.

Self-teaching.

This experiment asks whether a strong external teacher adds value beyond cheaper alternatives that reuse the student’s own backbone. We compare three teaching conditions against a no-skill baseline, all given identical task inputs and differing only in who produces the skills. In self-improvement, the student reflects on its own failures and writes its own skills, with no separate teacher. In self-aware teaching, a teacher reasons about the student but runs on the student’s own backbone, a low-cost stand-in for a strong teacher. In aware teaching, a strong external teacher model builds an explicit model of the student and generates skills from it. The setup has 36 task identities with two executions each, for 72 executions per condition. No-skill reaches 72.22%. Self-improvement reaches 81.94% (a gain of +9.7 points over no-skill, 95% CI [+1.4, +19.4]). Self-aware teaching reaches 79.17% (+6.9 points, 95% CI [−1.4,+18.1][-1.4,+18.1]). The external aware teacher reaches 83.33% (+11.1 points, 95% CI [+1.4, +23.6]). Self-improvement and aware teaching each clear zero over the baseline; self-aware does not. Same-backbone self-improvement is therefore a strong baseline. The external teacher’s margin over it is 1.39 points, which corresponds to one accepted execution out of 72, so on this single seed the advantage of the external teacher over self-improvement is small and should be read as exploratory. We also note that self-improvement incurred six skill-generation failures, whereas both teacher-driven conditions generated skills without errors.

Appendix F Student-Model Diagnostics with API Students

GPT-5.4-Mini records accepted analytical updates in every teaching round. Table 19 pairs its calibration scores with final task outcomes. Aware Brier is lower in two of three runs, and task accuracy is identical across the two teaching conditions within each run. For a strong student near ceiling, a better learner model improves prediction without changing the final score. This supports the teachability finding in Section 5.3.

Appendix G Extended Teaching and Skill Development

Configuration.

This experiment pairs Claude-Sonnet-5 with DeepSeek-V4-Flash in the compact planning harness with advice injection and matched retrieval. The frozen collection is generated at the hard difficulty setting with a fixed seed. It contains 40 teaching tasks, 12 development tasks, and 30 test tasks per suite across the same five suites. Eight rounds consume 200 distinct teaching tasks in batches of 25. Each condition executes every test task twice per round, so each rate averages 150 task scores.

Trajectory.

Table 20 reports acceptance and calibration for every round. Each teaching policy proposes three skills per round, and the log records 24 generation attempts with no generation failure in either condition. Aware analytical updates are accepted in all eight rounds, and the final analytical learner model holds five hypotheses and a measured inventory boundary. The fixed calibration panel uses ten task identities disjoint from the development tasks reserved for skill validation.

Paired intervals.

The final aware advantage over no skill is 6.3 points with a paired bootstrap interval of [2.0,11.0][2.0,11.0]. The agnostic advantage over no skill is 2.7 points with an interval of [−0.7,6.3][-0.7,6.3]. Only aware teaching separates from the untaught student. A direct comparison of aware with agnostic uses 100,000 paired task resamples, where each task keeps its two-execution mean under both conditions. It gives 3.7 points with a percentile interval of [0.0,7.7][0.0,7.7]. Thirteen tasks improve under aware teaching, six decline, and 131 are unchanged.

Where the gain arises.

Table 21 reports final acceptance by suite. Terminal tasks account for the advantage, contributing 4.7 points to the overall difference. Code is at ceiling under every condition, and mathematics and workflows are near ceiling.

Recursive renaming.

A sixth-round teaching attempt fails because a nested file remains unrenamed. The aware teacher then generates a skill that enumerates matching files recursively and verifies that no original extension remains. Its admission test succeeds on a matching development task where the empty-library execution fails. On the test set, all five renaming tasks pass in both aware executions during each of the final three rounds. A representative final aware trace enumerates the data/ tree with find, renames the discovered files, and checks for remaining matches. The corresponding agnostic trace uses a shallow glob and leaves a nested file unchanged.

Probe measurements enter skill content.

A third-round inventory probe succeeds at eight stock-keeping units and fails at twelve and sixteen. A fourth-round skill explicitly cites the observed twelve-item failure. It advises consolidated stock retrieval and progress tracking, with final verification deferred when the budget is tight. This is a direct link from a probe measurement to lesson content. Agnostic teaching also produces advice about reducing stock queries in this run. Inventory acceptance ends at 55.0% aware and 56.7% agnostic, since the procedure still requires one update call per deficient item. A later probe succeeds at all tested sizes through sixteen, so a sampled boundary should be read as conditional on the tested instances.

Curriculum composition.

The final agnostic library contains five learned and four generic skills. The aware library contains six learned and two generic skills, so aware teaching replaces more of its starting curriculum. Table 22 lists every learned skill with its native type and standalone admission utility. All six aware skills are process skills, while agnostic teaching produces two process and three content skills. Aware skills cover renaming and pipelines in addition to the inventory, merge, and discount categories covered by both. Their mean utility is 0.58 against 0.35 for agnostic skills. Both teachers write a discount procedure and a budget-aware inventory procedure, so both conditions discover some useful lessons.

Prediction quality.

The aware Brier score is lower than the agnostic score in every round on the fixed panel. It reaches its minimum of 0.046 in round three and stays between 0.063 and 0.079 afterward. The aware AUROC is 1.0 in rounds two through seven, so in those rounds the aware teacher separates the panel tasks its student will pass from those it will fail without error. The final skill-validation Brier scores are similar at 0.250 aware and 0.253 agnostic. Those measurements use changing candidate-dependent tasks and answer a different question from the fixed panel.

Cost.

The recorded teacher costs are $1.245 for aware teaching and $0.459 for agnostic teaching. Student costs are $0.812 and $0.739, and no-skill execution costs $0.562. These totals cover teaching and repeated evaluation across all eight rounds.

Appendix H Learner-Specificity Controls

H.1 Component ablations

Table 23 reports the component ablations on run S2 with their own no-skill and agnostic baselines. Each ablated aware teacher still exceeds both baselines in its job.

H.2 False-profile control

This control asks whether the teacher benefits from an accurate model of the specific student. The student is DeepSeek-V4-Flash and the teacher is Claude-Sonnet-5. The harness, frozen tasks, four teaching rounds, and admission procedure all stay fixed. Only the learner information supplied to the teacher changes. The overestimating profile describes the student as a frontier-class model comparable to GPT-5 or Claude-Opus-5. It claims near-ceiling competence across every task family, including tool use and long dependency chains. It also states that context loss and step limits are negligible, so repeated verification is cheap and most task families need little teaching. The underestimating profile gives the opposite description. It characterizes the student as comparable to a Qwen2-0.5B model with severe weaknesses in every skill from planning and arithmetic to state tracking. It tells the teacher that the learner needs highly explicit procedures, extensive decomposition, and detailed scaffolding. Both profiles stay frozen during teaching, so they remain wrong even as the teacher observes the real student’s trajectories.

Table 24 reports every round. Each run generates twelve candidates over four rounds without a generation failure, and none passes admission. All four final libraries therefore contain only the six generic seeds. Test acceptance still moves between rounds because each round re-executes the stochastic student. With a fixed generic library, final acceptance ranges from 71.7% to 82.5% across the four runs, which indicates the scale of evaluation noise at this sample size. The teacher costs per run are $0.364, $0.377, $0.394, and $0.408. The underestimating teacher’s AUROC falls below 0.5 in most rounds, so its predictions invert the ordering of the student’s real outcomes. The overestimating teacher ends with Brier between 0.19 and 0.29, several times the correct-profile value.

H.3 Library swap between students

This experiment asks whether a library fits the student it was written for. Two aware libraries come from the same teacher (Claude-Sonnet-5) and harness but different students, DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Gemini-3.8-Flash. At evaluation time we give each student its own library and the other student’s library on the same held-out tasks. Each direction shares one no-skill baseline and reports all three routes. Category routing reduces retrieval quality as a confound, so it most directly measures whether library content fits its student. Table 25 reports both libraries against the shared baseline. The pattern is reciprocal: each student does better with its own library in all six comparisons.

Appendix I Production Harnesses

Design.

We extended the framework to run Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and Pi through their native command-line interfaces while preserving each harness’s own execution workflow. All four harnesses use the same backbone through OpenRouter and receive the same frozen tasks, working-directory structure, execution budget, and evaluation procedure. We did not modify any internal planning loop, tool interface, or context-management policy. Changing them would turn the comparison into one between customized variants of each system. SAT interacts with each harness only through controls that a normal user has. Learned skills are supplied as natural-language context together with the task instruction. The harness remains responsible for interpreting the skill, choosing its native tools, and producing the output. The evaluation covers four suites (terminal, arithmetic, code, and dependent workflows) with twelve test tasks each and two executions per task. Teaching runs four rounds as in the main setting.

Results.

The harnesses differ from the base harness and from each other, so we report every result as a paired change against the same harness’s no-skill run in the same round. Table 26 gives the final-round changes with intervals, Table 27 gives these changes after every round, and Table 28 gives them by suite for the final round. Aware teaching ends at or above no skill in every harness. The largest risk appears in first-round agnostic libraries, which cost Pi 22.9 points and Codex 11.5 points before later rounds recover.

Appendix J Implementation and Measurement Details

Initialization and candidate lifecycle.

The six generic initial skills cover line counting, staged pipelines, inventory updates, and three other terminal categories. Learned skills with positive standalone utility can supersede a generic skill in the same category. The category cap sorts by utility and keeps two active skills. In S2, a third rename candidate has utility 1.0 and stays inactive under the two-skill category cap.

Execution summaries.

Result packages contain averaged final scores and compact execution summaries with tool counts. We use averaged task scores for all accuracy results and use tool-count summaries to illustrate behavior.

Budget accounting.

Table 29 reports mean role totals for S2 through S4 at the configured prices. Student totals include preparation, development, and repeated test evaluation. The aware teacher spends $0.39 per run, $0.16 more than the agnostic teacher. The untaught student produces more than twice the output tokens of either taught student, and the aware student produces 56% fewer output tokens even though its total also covers teaching and development executions. The complete aware condition costs $0.67 per run. Local-model accounting omits accelerator time.

Category outcomes.

Table 30 joins S2 through S4 to their task categories. Category means weight task records equally. The largest aware gains over agnostic teaching appear in extension renaming and function implementation.

Preparation data.

Each main run executes 60 distinct teaching records. Generation prompts expose subsets of task descriptions and trace summaries, and profiles and development feedback add further evidence. The 30 development records cover categories unevenly. Each run has one development task per terminal category and six inventory tasks, while code and arithmetic counts vary.

Evaluation protocol.

Every teaching round evaluates the same frozen test split, and unless otherwise stated, results report the final round. This fixes the reporting point in advance and avoids selecting the best intermediate score. A task’s score is the fraction of its two executions that the verifier accepts, so it is 0, 0.5, or 1. Acceptance is the mean task score over the held-out tasks, reported as a percentage, and run-level standard deviations are computed across runs.

Appendix K Amortizing Preparation Cost

For NN later tasks, the average model cost is

C¯​(N)=CprepareN+Cselect+Cexecute.\overline{C}(N)=\frac{C_{\mathrm{prepare}}}{N}+C_{\mathrm{select}}+C_{\mathrm{execute}}. (3)

If a directly deployed stronger agent costs CstrongC_{\mathrm{strong}} per task, teaching pays for itself once

N>CprepareCstrong−Cselect−Cexecute,N>\frac{C_{\mathrm{prepare}}}{C_{\mathrm{strong}}-C_{\mathrm{select}}-C_{\mathrm{execute}}}, (4)

given a positive denominator and acceptable accuracy. In the main setting, the aware teacher costs under one dollar per run. A deployment study under a common workload would measure both terms directly.
